extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, public-health professionals, and policymakers interested in the Flint water crisis
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style, comprehensive account of the Flint, Michigan water crisis covering timeline, testing results, studies, regulatory standards, investigations, and responses. The page compiles findings from studies, official reports, and news accounts about water quality, lead exposure, and related public-health and legal issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead and Copper Rule — requirement for optimized corrosion control treatment (CCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal Lead and Copper Rule requires 'optimized corrosion control treatment'. The Flint Water Advisory Task Force found that MDEQ failed to follow the federal Lead and Copper Rule and that the decision not to require CCT led directly to contamination of the Flint water system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CCT must be implemented to prevent lead leaching from pipes; failing to require/implement CCT (an anti-pattern cited in Flint) can directly cause lead contamination. The Task Force criticized a 'minimalist technical compliance approach' and concluded that not requiring CCT was a primary cause of the crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA sampling guidance — first-draw samples at taps in homes/buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA guidance requires that samples taken must be 'first-draw samples at taps in homes/buildings'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing that involves flushing taps for several minutes before sampling contravenes EPA guidance. Documentary claims that MDEQ staff took samples after flushing would violate this protocol and cast doubt on reported improvements in water quality. First-draw sampling is the standard for detecting lead that accumulates in plumbing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action level for lead in drinking water (15 ppb) and 90th-percentile compliance metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Safe Drinking Water Act Lead and Copper Rule the 'action level' for lead in water is 15 parts per billion (ppb); compliance is evaluated using the 90th percentile of samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Water systems must report 90th-percentile lead concentrations across sampled sites; if the 90th percentile exceeds 15 ppb, the system is in violation and must take corrective actions. Examples from Flint: state testing reported 90th-percentile readings above 15 ppb in some monitoring periods and below 15 ppb in later periods. The 90th-percentile metric is central to regulatory determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal sampling protocol — target homes with lead plumbing/service lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal rules require that water systems 'seek out homes with lead plumbing for testing' (i.e., prioritize sampling in homes most at risk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to target homes with known or likely lead service lines (an anti-pattern noted in Flint) can lead to underestimation of lead levels. The Flint documents show the city did not know locations of lead service lines and thereby 'disregarded federal rules' about targeted sampling, which likely skewed results toward underestimating contamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sentinel-site versus voluntary/homeowner-driven sampling and representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Different sampling programs (state 'sentinel' sites vs voluntary/homeowner-driven sampling) yield different results; voluntary sampling often showed more exceedances than sentinel-site testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentinel-site sampling (regulated monitoring sites) may underrepresent true exposure if sites are not representative of the most at-risk homes; homeowner-driven voluntary sampling can reveal higher lead occurrences but does not conform to Lead and Copper Rule monitoring requirements. Interpreters should consider sampling methodology when comparing results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blood lead level threshold used in public-health studies (>5 micrograms per deciliter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies cited (e.g., Hanna-Attisha at Hurley Medical Center) used a blood-lead threshold of above five micrograms per deciliter (5 μg/dL) to define elevated blood lead levels in children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers and public-health assessments commonly use >5 μg/dL as an indicator of elevated pediatric blood-lead exposure. Study comparisons should account for sampling frame differences (e.g., which children were screened) and demographic confounders; limitations (like non-universal screening) can skew estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: CDC guidance — no safe level of lead exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 'there is no safe level of lead exposure in water that people can consume' and lead can be harmful at very low concentrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health policy should assume that any detectable lead is potentially harmful, with special concern for children (risks include anemia, impaired growth, neurodevelopmental and behavioral problems). This principle argues for precautionary actions even when regulatory action levels are not exceeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory monitoring periods and timing for corrosion-control decisions (two six-month monitoring periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory practice referenced: some agencies sought to delay decisions on corrosion control until completion of 'two six-month periods of sampling' under Lead and Copper Rule procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While monitoring period aggregation is part of compliance assessment, delaying implementation of corrosion control pending multiple monitoring cycles can be an anti-pattern if public-health risk indicators already exist. The EPA and critics argued for more immediate action in Flint rather than waiting multiple monitoring periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthophosphate/corrosion inhibitor addition to rebuild pipe lining and reduce lead leaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition of orthophosphate (a corrosion inhibitor) to the water supply is a treatment used to rebuild pipe lining and reduce lead release from plumbing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementing orthophosphate dosing is a recognized remedial action to reduce pipe corrosion and lead leaching; Flint added orthophosphate after reconnection to Detroit water and as part of mitigation. Failure to add inhibitors when switching to a more corrosive source is a contributory factor to lead release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microbiological/epidemiological linkage standards for disease outbreak attribution (genetic matching of isolates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Linking Legionnaires' disease cases to water requires microbiological and epidemiological evidence, including genetic matches between clinical isolates and environmental (water) isolates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits and studies in Flint relied on genetic links and outbreak investigations to support an association between the water-source change/management and increased Legionella cases. Investigations should consider multiple possible sources and use molecular typing, exposure histories, and environmental sampling to attribute outbreaks; focusing on a single source can miss other contributors.
